author: Times News
description:
“What we see here is a continuation of everything to do with peace talks in the past year and a bit, which is just more an act of theatre rather than real intention to stop the fighting.”

The short 32-hour Orthodox Easter ceasefire announced between Russia and Ukraine is unlikely to make any real difference on the ground, with both sides continuing strikes and drone attacks and showing little genuine intent to pause the war, says Kyiv Independent reporter Francis Farrell.

Francis Farrell was speaking to Kate Gerbeau and Peter Cardwell on Times Radio Breakfast. Listen live every weekend 6–10am.

author: Times News
description:
Having first demanded that Iran 'open the fucking strait', President Trump followed up with a post vowing 'an entire civilisation will die tonight' if it did not do so. 

But could any such order ever be legal, and would the American military even agree to carry it out?

Patrick and Tom chew over these and other questions, including whether it's time for America's long-standing allies to bail on it, if bombing a country into submission ever works, and what the sacking of the head of the US army tells us about the state of the country's military and, perhaps, its constitution. 

But first up, in a week which saw possibly the finest rescue mission ever carried out, John Nichols recalls his experience in the first Gulf War of being shot down over enemy territory, attempting to evade capture, and waiting for the infantry to arrive. 

Hosts: General Sir Patrick Sanders and Tom Newton Dunn

Guest: John Nichol

Producer: Micaela Arneson

Executive producer: Fiona Leach

Image: Getty

title: Can A President Legally Order The Death Of A 'Whole Civilisation'?

author: Times News
description:
The internal conflict in Iran extends far beyond geopolitical borders, manifesting as a profound ideological schism within the domestic sphere. Majid Parsa, an Iranian doctor living in London, provides a rare glimpse into a household fractured by opposing loyalties to the Islamic Republic. His narrative traces the evolution of a family from the fervour of the 1979 Revolution to the contemporary disillusionment following decades of state-sanctioned oppression.
